text:
The European Shipowners Association (ECSA) and Airlines 4 Europe (A4E) have called on the EU to channel emissions trading system (ETS) revenues into sustainable fuels and technologies.

Shipping and aviation already contribute over €11bn ($12.57bn) to EU ETS revenues annually.

“As a priority, this money must be channelled into de-risking investment in sustainable fuels that are today on average four times more expensive for shipping and three to six times more expensive for aviation than conventional fuels,” it said in a joint statement.

“Bridging the price gap between sustainable and conventional fuels is key to increasing their availability on the market. The European Commission should require EU Member States to earmark at least part of their ETS revenues for the uptake and availability of sustainable fuels for shipping and aviation, and to incentivise them to top up any existing EU mechanisms with national ETS revenues.”

European shipowners are leading global investments in sustainable fuel-powered vessels, with 44% of the global orderbook, but Europe’s fuel availability is not keeping pace.

Asia leads with 74% of fuel production projects, while Europe accounts for just 10%.

Less than 5% of European sustainable fuel production is currently intended for maritime use, according to Sotiris Raptis, Secretary General of the ECSA.

He said revenues should be used at EU and national level to bridge the price gap and support sustainable fuel availability and clean tech projects, which is key for the energy transition of the sector and continent’s energy security.

European airlines contributed €2.3bn ($2.6bn) to EU ETS in 2024 alone – a figure set to exceed €5bn ($5.7bn) annually by 2030. Yet the revenues are not being recycled back into the fuels and technologies airlines need to decarbonise.

The EU does not channel all ETS revenues into sustainable fuels because member states retain the authority to spend these funds, and many prioritise general budget needs over sector-specific green investment.

While the EU requires member states to spend their ETS revenues on climate-related activities, they are not legally mandated to earmark them specifically for sustainable fuels.

In the aviation sector, the 20 million sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) allowances on the table fall short of 2030 demand, and without clarity on post-2030 availability, the investment case simply does not stack up.

The UK government has launched a consultation to stress test its own SAF mandate, asking the industry whether enough e-fuels, including hydrogen-derived power-to-liquids will be available to meet future requirements.

Yet there are signs green hydrogen-based SAF offtake deals are ramping up ahead of incoming mandates.

“Airlines – and ultimately passengers – are paying into a system that is not working for them – or for the climate. Investing ETS revenues in fuel availability and offtakes is essential for decarbonising shipping and aviation and Europe’s energy security,” said Ourania Georgoutsakou, Managing Director of A4E.

The Middle East-induced energy crisis and push to protect European industrial competitiveness have led some nations to push for a suspension of the ETS, arguing that high carbon costs are driving businesses out of Europe.

text:
Perth Airport has engaged Duratec Limited and West Coast Civil Pty Ltd as the Joint Venture (DWJV) to deliver early contractor involvement (ECI) services for the Jet Fuel Expansion Program.

The ECI phase will progress the project through concept design, supporting the development of critical aviation fuel infrastructure as part of Perth Airport’s multi‑billion-dollar expansion program. The ECI phase is expected to run for approximately six months.

Perth Airport’s chief planning and projects officer, Steve Moreland, said the project will provide initial concept development for future fuel distribution across the estate: “Following our acquisition of the on airport current jet fuel storage and distribution infrastructure, Perth Airport is now investing further to strengthen capacity and support the continued growth of Western Australia’s aviation sector,” he said.

“Reliable and efficient fuel infrastructure is essential to enable future growth at Perth Airport. The Jet Fuel Expansion Program forms a key component of Perth Airport’s long-term development, which will consolidate commercial passenger services into a central precinct while enhancing critical enabling infrastructure. DWJV joins our project with a strong multidisciplinary construction led team with proven strengths in project management, design and constructability. We’re especially excited to be working with local companies such as Duratec and West Coast Civil to deliver our One Airport vision.”

Duratec’s managing director, Chris Oates, said the Duratec and West Coast Civil partnership was built on proven expertise, experience, and local commitment: “As Australia’s fourth largest airport, Perth Airport plays a pivotal role in supporting the economic growth of Western Australia,” said Oates. “Duratec and West Coast Civil will be amongst the first contractors to bring this critical infrastructure program to life. We’re committed to achieving the best possible outcomes for Perth Airport, supporting its long-term development, which will strengthen essential infrastructure to meet future demand.”

SAF vs Electrification Background and Objectives

The aviation industry faces unprecedented pressure to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, driving an urgent need to evaluate alternative propulsion technologies. Two primary pathways have emerged as leading contenders for decarbonizing aviation: Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and aircraft electrification. This technological crossroads represents one of the most critical decisions facing the aerospace sector, with implications extending far beyond environmental considerations to encompass economic viability, operational feasibility, and long-term industry transformation.

SAF represents an evolutionary approach that leverages existing aircraft infrastructure while providing immediate carbon reduction benefits. Derived from renewable feedstocks including waste oils, agricultural residues, and synthetic processes, SAF can achieve up to 80% lifecycle carbon reduction compared to conventional jet fuel. The technology builds upon decades of turbine engine development and existing fuel distribution networks, offering a pathway that requires minimal modifications to current aircraft designs and airport infrastructure.

Aircraft electrification, conversely, represents a revolutionary shift toward zero-emission flight through battery-powered or hybrid-electric propulsion systems. This approach promises complete elimination of direct carbon emissions and significantly reduced operational costs through lower energy prices and simplified maintenance requirements. However, electrification faces substantial technical barriers related to energy density limitations, charging infrastructure requirements, and fundamental physics constraints that currently restrict applications to short-range, small aircraft segments.

The scalability challenge differs fundamentally between these approaches. SAF scalability hinges on feedstock availability, production capacity expansion, and cost reduction through economies of scale. Current global SAF production represents less than 0.1% of aviation fuel demand, requiring massive industrial scaling to meet projected needs. Electrification scalability depends on breakthrough advances in battery technology, with current energy densities approximately 40 times lower than jet fuel, limiting practical applications to aircraft under 100 seats on routes shorter than 500 nautical miles.

Return on investment considerations encompass both direct financial metrics and broader economic impacts. SAF investments focus on production facility development, feedstock supply chains, and distribution infrastructure, with payback periods heavily influenced by carbon pricing mechanisms and regulatory mandates. Electrification investments concentrate on battery technology development, charging infrastructure deployment, and aircraft redesign, with potential for superior long-term returns in applicable market segments due to dramatically lower operational costs.

The strategic objective of this analysis centers on determining optimal investment allocation between these competing technologies while considering their respective scalability trajectories and financial viability across different aviation market segments.

Aviation Decarbonization Market Demand Analysis

The aviation industry faces unprecedented pressure to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, driven by increasingly stringent regulatory frameworks and growing environmental consciousness among stakeholders. The International Civil Aviation Organization's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation has established mandatory carbon offsetting requirements, while regional regulations such as the European Union's Emissions Trading System are expanding to include aviation sectors. These regulatory pressures are creating substantial market demand for decarbonization solutions.

Commercial airlines are experiencing mounting pressure from investors, customers, and regulatory bodies to demonstrate concrete progress toward sustainability goals. Major carriers have committed to ambitious carbon neutrality targets, with many pledging to achieve net-zero emissions within the next two decades. This commitment translates into significant capital allocation toward decarbonization technologies, creating a robust market foundation for both sustainable aviation fuel and electrification solutions.

The market demand exhibits distinct characteristics across different aviation segments. Commercial long-haul aviation represents the largest market opportunity due to high fuel consumption volumes and limited near-term alternatives to liquid fuels. Regional and short-haul flights present opportunities for both sustainable aviation fuel adoption and electric aircraft deployment, with market preferences varying based on route characteristics and operational requirements.

Corporate sustainability mandates are driving demand from business aviation and cargo sectors, where companies seek to reduce scope 3 emissions associated with air transport. This segment demonstrates willingness to pay premium prices for sustainable solutions, creating early adoption opportunities that can drive technology maturation and cost reduction.

Infrastructure investment patterns reveal strong market confidence in decarbonization technologies. Airport authorities are investing in sustainable aviation fuel supply infrastructure, while simultaneously preparing for electric aircraft operations through charging infrastructure development. These parallel investments indicate market recognition that multiple decarbonization pathways will coexist rather than compete exclusively.

Market demand is further amplified by supply chain sustainability requirements, where manufacturers and logistics companies face pressure to decarbonize their entire value chains. This creates cascading demand effects throughout the aviation ecosystem, from passenger transport to cargo operations, establishing a comprehensive market foundation for sustainable aviation technologies.

Current SAF and Electric Aviation Technology Status

Sustainable Aviation Fuel technology has reached commercial viability with several production pathways demonstrating operational success. The most mature approach involves Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA), which converts waste oils and fats into jet fuel through hydrogenation processes. This technology currently produces SAF at approximately 2-3 times the cost of conventional jet fuel, with production facilities operational in the United States, Europe, and Asia. Major refineries have integrated HEFA units with capacities ranging from 10,000 to 100,000 barrels per day.

Fischer-Tropsch synthesis represents another established SAF production method, utilizing biomass gasification to create synthetic fuels. While technically proven, this pathway faces higher capital expenditure requirements and energy intensity challenges. Current facilities demonstrate conversion efficiencies of 45-55%, with ongoing research targeting 65% efficiency through advanced catalyst systems and process optimization.

Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) technology has progressed from laboratory scale to demonstration facilities, converting ethanol or butanol into aviation fuel. Recent breakthroughs in catalyst development have improved yield rates to 85-90%, making this pathway increasingly attractive for regions with established biofuel infrastructure. Power-to-Liquid (PtL) technology remains in early commercial phases, requiring significant renewable electricity inputs but offering carbon-neutral fuel production potential.

Electric aviation technology exhibits stark performance variations across aircraft categories. Battery energy density currently reaches 250-300 Wh/kg in commercial aviation applications, sufficient for aircraft under 19 passengers on routes shorter than 200 nautical miles. Leading manufacturers have achieved certification for electric training aircraft and are conducting flight testing of commuter aircraft with 9-19 seat configurations.

Hybrid-electric propulsion systems demonstrate greater near-term scalability, combining conventional engines with electric motors to reduce fuel consumption by 20-30% on regional routes. These systems address range limitations while providing operational flexibility during the transition period. Battery thermal management and charging infrastructure represent critical technical challenges requiring standardized solutions across airport networks.

Hydrogen fuel cell technology for aviation remains largely experimental, with prototype aircraft demonstrating flight capabilities but facing significant infrastructure and storage challenges. Current fuel cell systems achieve power-to-weight ratios of 1-2 kW/kg, substantially below the 5-8 kW/kg required for commercial aviation applications.

The regulatory landscape shows divergent approval timelines, with SAF achieving widespread certification under existing fuel specifications, while electric aircraft face extended certification processes requiring new airworthiness standards and pilot training protocols.

Existing SAF Production and Electric Propulsion Solutions

01 Sustainable aviation fuel production and processing technologies

Technologies focused on the development and production of sustainable aviation fuels through various feedstock sources and conversion processes. These innovations include advanced refining techniques, bio-based fuel synthesis, and alternative fuel production methods that reduce carbon emissions while maintaining aviation performance standards. The technologies encompass feedstock preparation, catalytic conversion, and fuel quality optimization processes.

Sustainable aviation fuel production and processing technologies: Advanced methods for producing sustainable aviation fuels from various feedstocks including biomass, waste materials, and synthetic pathways. These technologies focus on improving fuel quality, reducing production costs, and enhancing the conversion efficiency of raw materials into aviation-grade fuels that meet industry specifications.

Aircraft electrification systems and hybrid propulsion: Development of electric and hybrid-electric propulsion systems for aircraft, including battery technologies, electric motors, and power management systems. These innovations aim to reduce emissions and fuel consumption while maintaining operational performance and safety standards for various aircraft types.

Economic optimization and return on investment analysis: Methods and systems for evaluating the financial viability and economic benefits of sustainable aviation technologies. This includes cost-benefit analysis frameworks, investment optimization strategies, and economic modeling tools to assess the profitability and market potential of green aviation solutions.

Scalability assessment and infrastructure development: Technologies and methodologies for scaling up sustainable aviation fuel production and electrification infrastructure. This encompasses supply chain optimization, manufacturing scale-up processes, and infrastructure planning to support widespread adoption of sustainable aviation technologies.

Integration and operational efficiency systems: Comprehensive systems for integrating sustainable aviation fuels and electric propulsion technologies into existing aviation operations. These solutions focus on optimizing fuel management, energy distribution, and operational workflows to maximize efficiency and minimize environmental impact while ensuring regulatory compliance.

02 Aircraft electrification systems and hybrid propulsion

Electric propulsion systems and hybrid aircraft technologies that integrate electric motors, battery systems, and power management solutions for aviation applications. These systems focus on reducing fuel consumption and emissions through electrification of aircraft propulsion, including electric motors, energy storage systems, and power distribution networks designed for aviation environments.

Expand Specific Solutions

03 Energy storage and battery technologies for aviation

Advanced battery systems and energy storage solutions specifically designed for aviation applications, including high-energy density batteries, thermal management systems, and charging infrastructure. These technologies address the unique requirements of aviation environments such as weight constraints, safety standards, and operational reliability while providing sufficient energy capacity for electric aircraft operations.

Methods and systems for analyzing the economic viability and return on investment of sustainable aviation fuel and electrification projects. These approaches include cost-benefit analysis frameworks, lifecycle economic modeling, and financial optimization strategies that evaluate the scalability and profitability of sustainable aviation technologies while considering operational costs, infrastructure investments, and market dynamics.

05 Infrastructure and scalability solutions for sustainable aviation

Infrastructure development and scalability frameworks for implementing sustainable aviation fuel and electrification technologies on a commercial scale. These solutions address supply chain management, distribution networks, charging infrastructure, and production scaling challenges. The technologies focus on creating integrated systems that can support widespread adoption of sustainable aviation technologies across different operational scales.

Expand Specific Solutions

Major Players in SAF and Electric Aviation Sectors

The sustainable aviation fuel versus electrification debate represents a rapidly evolving competitive landscape within the aviation decarbonization sector. The industry is currently in a transitional phase, with the global sustainable aviation fuel market projected to reach $15 billion by 2030, while electric aviation remains largely in development stages. Technology maturity varies significantly between approaches: SAF producers like Neste Oyj and LanzaJet have achieved commercial-scale production and airline partnerships, while electrification pioneers such as Ampaire and Ascendance Flight Technologies are still conducting prototype testing. Traditional aerospace giants including Airbus Operations, General Electric, and Embraer are hedging strategies across both pathways. The competitive dynamics show SAF gaining near-term traction due to infrastructure compatibility, while electrification faces scalability challenges but offers superior long-term efficiency potential for short-haul applications.

Ampaire, Inc.

Technical Solution: Ampaire focuses on electric aircraft development for regional aviation, developing hybrid-electric and fully electric aircraft solutions. Their EL-series aircraft targets short-haul flights with battery-electric propulsion systems, addressing the electrification pathway for aviation decarbonization. The company's approach emphasizes modular battery systems and distributed electric propulsion to optimize efficiency and safety. Ampaire's business model focuses on regional routes where electric aircraft can be commercially viable with current battery technology, providing a stepping stone toward broader aviation electrification as battery energy density improves.

Strengths: Purpose-built electric aircraft design, focus on commercially viable short-haul routes, innovative propulsion architecture. Weaknesses: Limited range and payload capacity, battery technology constraints, charging infrastructure requirements, regulatory certification challenges.

Shell Internationale Research Maatschappij BV

Technical Solution: Shell has invested heavily in both SAF production through their renewable fuels facilities and electric aviation technologies. Their SAF strategy focuses on converting waste cooking oil and other sustainable feedstocks into jet fuel using advanced refining processes. Shell operates biofuel production facilities capable of producing SAF at commercial scale and has partnerships with airlines for supply agreements. Additionally, Shell is exploring power-to-liquids technology for synthetic SAF production using renewable electricity and captured CO2, addressing scalability concerns through diversified production pathways.

Strengths: Integrated energy company with existing refining infrastructure, diversified technology portfolio, strong financial resources for scaling. Weaknesses: High capital investment requirements, competition with other renewable fuel applications, regulatory uncertainty affecting ROI projections.

Aviation Environmental Policy and Regulatory Framework

The aviation industry operates within an increasingly complex regulatory landscape that significantly influences the adoption pathways for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and electrification technologies. International frameworks established by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) serve as the foundation for global environmental standards, with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) representing the most comprehensive regulatory mechanism to date.

CORSIA mandates carbon-neutral growth from 2020 levels for international aviation, creating substantial market drivers for both SAF deployment and electric aircraft development. The scheme's three-phase implementation approach provides flexibility for airlines to choose between offsetting, SAF utilization, or fleet electrification based on route characteristics and operational requirements. This regulatory structure inherently favors solutions with demonstrated scalability and favorable return on investment profiles.

Regional regulatory frameworks exhibit varying degrees of ambition and implementation timelines. The European Union's ReFuelEU Aviation initiative mandates specific SAF blending requirements, starting at 2% by 2025 and escalating to 63% by 2050, with sub-mandates for synthetic fuels. These binding targets create predictable demand signals that enhance SAF investment attractiveness despite current cost premiums. Simultaneously, the EU's taxonomy regulation provides green financing advantages for qualifying sustainable aviation technologies.

United States federal policy emphasizes market-based incentives through the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Grand Challenge and various tax credit mechanisms. The Inflation Reduction Act extends SAF production credits while establishing new incentives for sustainable aviation technology development. State-level initiatives, particularly in California through the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, create additional revenue streams that improve SAF economic viability in specific markets.

Emerging regulatory trends indicate increasing focus on lifecycle carbon accounting and technology-neutral approaches to emissions reduction. Aviation authorities are developing certification frameworks for electric aircraft operations, with the Federal Aviation Administration and European Union Aviation Safety Agency establishing parallel pathways for electric propulsion system approval. These regulatory developments directly impact the comparative scalability potential between SAF and electrification strategies.

The regulatory environment creates distinct competitive advantages for each technology pathway. SAF benefits from immediate applicability to existing fleet operations and established certification processes, while electrification faces longer regulatory approval timelines but potentially greater long-term policy support for zero-emission technologies. Understanding these regulatory dynamics remains crucial for accurate ROI projections and strategic technology investment decisions.

Economic Viability and Investment Return Analysis

The economic viability of sustainable aviation fuel versus electrification presents distinct investment profiles with varying capital requirements and return timelines. SAF production facilities require substantial upfront investments ranging from $500 million to $2 billion for commercial-scale refineries, depending on feedstock type and production technology. The capital intensity is particularly high for advanced biofuel facilities utilizing waste materials or synthetic fuel production through power-to-liquid processes.

Electrification pathways demand different investment structures, with battery technology representing the largest cost component. Current lithium-ion battery costs have decreased to approximately $130 per kWh, yet aviation applications require energy densities exceeding 500 Wh/kg for viable commercial operations. Infrastructure investments for electric aircraft include charging stations, grid upgrades, and specialized maintenance facilities, with estimated costs of $50-100 million per major airport hub.

Return on investment calculations reveal contrasting scenarios for each technology path. SAF production facilities typically achieve break-even points within 8-12 years, assuming stable feedstock supply and carbon credit mechanisms. The revenue model benefits from existing aircraft compatibility and established fuel distribution networks, reducing market entry barriers and accelerating cash flow generation.

Electric aviation investments face longer payback periods due to current technological limitations and market uncertainties. However, operational cost advantages become significant once technology maturity is achieved, with electricity costs representing 60-70% savings compared to conventional jet fuel on an energy-equivalent basis. The total cost of ownership for electric aircraft shows favorable projections for short-haul routes under 500 nautical miles.

Risk assessment indicates that SAF investments carry lower technological risks but face feedstock availability constraints and regulatory uncertainties regarding carbon pricing mechanisms. Electrification investments present higher technological risks, particularly regarding battery performance and safety certification, yet offer greater long-term cost reduction potential and regulatory support through environmental mandates.

Financial modeling suggests that hybrid investment strategies may optimize risk-adjusted returns, with SAF providing near-term revenue generation while electrification investments position for future market dominance in specific aviation segments.

Municipal Waste to SAF Conversion Background and Objectives

The aviation industry faces mounting pressure to reduce its carbon footprint, with greenhouse gas emissions from commercial aviation accounting for approximately 2-3% of global CO2 emissions. Traditional jet fuel dependency on fossil resources presents significant environmental challenges, driving urgent demand for sustainable alternatives. Municipal solid waste (MSW) represents an abundant, underutilized feedstock that could simultaneously address waste management challenges while producing renewable aviation fuel.

Municipal waste generation continues escalating globally, with developed nations producing 1.2-2.1 kg per capita daily. Current waste management systems predominantly rely on landfilling and incineration, both presenting environmental concerns including methane emissions and air pollution. Converting MSW into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) offers a circular economy solution that transforms waste streams into valuable energy resources.

The International Civil Aviation Organization has established ambitious targets requiring 5% SAF adoption by 2030, creating substantial market demand for alternative fuel sources. Current SAF production primarily depends on vegetable oils, used cooking oil, and agricultural residues, which face supply limitations and potential food security conflicts. MSW-derived SAF could provide a complementary pathway without competing with food production systems.

Technological advancement in thermochemical and biochemical conversion processes has demonstrated feasibility for transforming heterogeneous waste streams into high-quality aviation fuel. Gasification, pyrolysis, and fermentation technologies show promising potential for processing organic waste fractions while managing non-organic components effectively. These processes can achieve fuel specifications meeting ASTM D7566 standards for commercial aviation applications.

The primary objective involves developing efficient conversion technologies that can process mixed municipal waste streams while maintaining consistent fuel quality parameters. Key technical targets include achieving energy conversion efficiencies exceeding 40%, producing SAF with lifecycle carbon intensity reductions of at least 50% compared to conventional jet fuel, and establishing economically viable processing costs below $3 per gallon.

Secondary objectives encompass optimizing feedstock preparation methods to handle waste heterogeneity, developing robust purification systems for fuel quality assurance, and creating integrated waste-to-fuel facilities that maximize resource recovery while minimizing environmental impact. These technological developments aim to establish MSW-to-SAF conversion as a scalable, commercially viable pathway supporting both aviation decarbonization and sustainable waste management goals.

Market Demand Analysis for Sustainable Aviation Fuel

The global aviation industry faces mounting pressure to reduce carbon emissions, with sustainable aviation fuel emerging as the most viable near-term solution for decarbonization. Current aviation accounts for approximately 2-3% of global CO2 emissions, with projections indicating substantial growth in air travel demand over the coming decades. This creates an urgent need for alternative fuel sources that can significantly reduce lifecycle carbon emissions while maintaining compatibility with existing aircraft engines and infrastructure.

Sustainable aviation fuel derived from municipal waste represents a particularly compelling market opportunity due to the dual benefit of waste management and clean fuel production. The aviation sector's commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 has intensified demand for SAF across all market segments, from commercial airlines to cargo carriers and private aviation. Major airlines are increasingly entering into long-term purchase agreements for sustainable aviation fuel, creating a stable demand foundation for producers.

The regulatory landscape strongly supports SAF market expansion through various policy mechanisms. The European Union's ReFuelEU Aviation initiative mandates increasing SAF blending requirements, starting at 2% by 2025 and reaching 63% by 2050. Similar regulatory frameworks are emerging globally, including the United States' Sustainable Aviation Fuel Grand Challenge and various national-level incentive programs that provide production tax credits and blending mandates.

Municipal waste-derived SAF addresses critical supply chain challenges facing the aviation industry. Traditional SAF production relies heavily on limited feedstock sources such as used cooking oil and agricultural residues, creating supply constraints and price volatility. Municipal solid waste offers a more abundant and geographically distributed feedstock base, potentially enabling larger-scale production facilities closer to major aviation hubs.

The economic drivers for waste-to-SAF conversion extend beyond fuel production revenues. Municipalities face increasing costs for waste management and landfill operations, while simultaneously seeking solutions to reduce methane emissions from waste disposal. Converting municipal waste into aviation fuel creates additional revenue streams for waste management operators while addressing environmental compliance requirements.

Market analysis indicates strong growth potential across multiple aviation segments. Commercial aviation represents the largest volume opportunity, driven by fleet expansion and regulatory compliance requirements. Cargo aviation shows particularly strong demand due to the sector's emphasis on sustainability credentials for logistics customers. Business and private aviation segments demonstrate willingness to pay premium prices for sustainable fuel options, providing attractive early-market opportunities for waste-derived SAF producers.

Current Status and Challenges in Waste-to-SAF Technologies

The conversion of municipal waste into sustainable aviation fuel represents a promising yet technically challenging pathway that has gained significant momentum in recent years. Current waste-to-SAF technologies primarily rely on thermochemical and biochemical conversion processes, with gasification-to-Fischer-Tropsch synthesis and pyrolysis-to-upgrading being the most mature approaches. Several demonstration plants worldwide have successfully produced SAF from municipal solid waste, including Fulcrum BioEnergy's Sierra facility in Nevada and Velocys' projects in the United States and United Kingdom.

The feedstock preparation stage presents substantial challenges due to the heterogeneous nature of municipal waste. Effective sorting, cleaning, and preprocessing systems are essential to remove contaminants such as metals, glass, and chlorinated materials that can poison catalysts or produce harmful emissions. Current preprocessing technologies achieve contamination levels suitable for conversion, but the energy intensity and operational costs remain significant barriers to commercial viability.

Thermochemical conversion pathways face several technical hurdles, particularly in maintaining consistent syngas quality from variable waste feedstocks. Temperature control, residence time optimization, and catalyst performance under fluctuating operating conditions continue to challenge system reliability. The Fischer-Tropsch synthesis step requires precise H2/CO ratios, which are difficult to maintain when processing diverse waste streams with varying moisture content and chemical composition.

Biochemical conversion routes, while potentially more selective, struggle with the complex lignocellulosic structures present in waste paper and organic fractions. Pretreatment methods to enhance enzymatic accessibility often require harsh chemicals or extreme conditions, increasing process complexity and environmental impact. Fermentation efficiency remains suboptimal due to inhibitory compounds generated during pretreatment and the presence of competing microorganisms in waste-derived substrates.

Product upgrading and purification represent critical bottlenecks in achieving aviation fuel specifications. Current hydrotreating and isomerization technologies can produce SAF meeting ASTM D7566 standards, but yield losses during upgrading reduce overall process efficiency. The removal of heteroatoms, particularly nitrogen and sulfur compounds originating from waste proteins and synthetic materials, requires intensive hydrogen consumption and specialized catalysts.

Economic viability remains the most significant challenge, with current production costs exceeding conventional jet fuel by 2-3 times. Capital expenditure requirements for integrated waste-to-SAF facilities range from $300-500 million, while operational expenses are driven by feedstock preprocessing, catalyst replacement, and utility consumption. Regulatory uncertainties regarding waste classification, emission standards, and fuel certification pathways further complicate commercial deployment strategies.

Existing Municipal Waste to SAF Conversion Solutions

01 Waste-to-energy conversion technologies

Advanced thermal and biological conversion processes that transform municipal solid waste into valuable energy products such as electricity, heat, and fuel. These technologies include gasification, pyrolysis, and anaerobic digestion systems that maximize energy recovery while minimizing environmental impact. The processes are designed to handle various waste compositions and optimize energy output through controlled temperature and pressure conditions.

Waste-to-energy conversion technologies: Advanced thermal and biological processes for converting municipal solid waste into usable energy forms such as electricity, heat, or fuel. These technologies include gasification, pyrolysis, and anaerobic digestion systems that can efficiently process various waste streams while reducing environmental impact and generating valuable energy outputs.

Waste sorting and separation systems: Automated and mechanical systems designed to separate different types of municipal waste materials for improved recycling and processing efficiency. These systems utilize various technologies including optical sorting, magnetic separation, and density-based separation to categorize waste streams and enhance material recovery rates.

Organic waste treatment and composting: Biological treatment processes specifically designed for organic fraction of municipal waste, including composting systems, biogas generation, and organic matter decomposition technologies. These methods focus on converting biodegradable waste into useful products while minimizing landfill requirements and environmental pollution.

Waste processing equipment and machinery: Specialized mechanical equipment and apparatus for handling, processing, and treating municipal waste materials. This includes shredders, compactors, conveyor systems, and other industrial machinery designed to improve waste processing efficiency and reduce operational costs in waste management facilities.

Environmental monitoring and quality control: Systems and methods for monitoring environmental parameters and ensuring quality standards during municipal waste processing operations. These technologies include emission monitoring, leachate treatment, air quality control, and environmental impact assessment tools to maintain compliance with environmental regulations.

02 Advanced sorting and separation systems

Automated mechanical and optical sorting technologies that enhance the quality of recyclable materials recovered from municipal waste streams. These systems utilize sensors, artificial intelligence, and robotic mechanisms to identify and separate different waste components with high precision. The technology improves material purity and reduces contamination in recycled products.

Expand Specific Solutions

03 Biological treatment and composting processes

Engineered biological systems that decompose organic municipal waste into high-quality compost and soil amendments. These processes involve controlled aerobic and anaerobic decomposition using specific microorganisms and optimized environmental conditions. The resulting products meet quality standards for agricultural and landscaping applications while reducing landfill burden.

Expand Specific Solutions

04 Chemical recycling and material recovery

Advanced chemical processes that break down complex waste materials into their molecular components for reuse in manufacturing new products. These technologies handle plastics, textiles, and other synthetic materials that are difficult to process through conventional recycling methods. The processes produce high-purity raw materials that can replace virgin resources in industrial applications.

Expand Specific Solutions

05 Integrated waste management systems

Comprehensive platforms that combine multiple treatment technologies and digital monitoring systems to optimize municipal waste processing efficiency. These integrated approaches include real-time tracking, automated process control, and data analytics to maximize resource recovery and minimize environmental impact. The systems are designed for scalability and adaptability to different municipal requirements.

Expand Specific Solutions

Key Players in Waste-to-SAF Industry

The municipal waste-to-sustainable aviation fuel sector represents an emerging market at the intersection of waste management and renewable energy, currently in its early commercialization phase with significant growth potential driven by aviation decarbonization mandates. The market demonstrates substantial scale opportunities given global municipal waste generation exceeding 2 billion tons annually and aviation's urgent need for sustainable fuel alternatives. Technology maturity varies considerably across the competitive landscape, with established players like Fulcrum BioEnergy and Eni SpA advancing thermochemical conversion processes toward commercial deployment, while research institutions including Tianjin University, North Carolina State University, and King Abdullah University of Science & Technology drive fundamental innovation in conversion pathways. Chinese companies such as Tus Environmental Science & Technology and Wuhan Tianhe Technology leverage extensive waste processing infrastructure, though most participants remain in pilot or demonstration phases, indicating the technology requires further development before widespread commercial viability.

Tianjin University

Technical Solution: Tianjin University has developed innovative catalytic pyrolysis technology for converting municipal organic waste into sustainable aviation fuel precursors. Their research focuses on developing novel zeolite-based catalysts that can selectively convert waste-derived bio-oil into aviation fuel range hydrocarbons through catalytic cracking and upgrading processes. The technology involves two-stage processing: initial fast pyrolysis of sorted organic municipal waste at 450-500°C to produce bio-oil, followed by catalytic upgrading using their proprietary catalyst systems to produce jet fuel components. Their process achieves bio-oil yields of 60-65% from organic waste feedstock and subsequent upgrading efficiency of 70-75% to aviation fuel range products. The university has demonstrated pilot-scale operations processing 100kg/day of municipal organic waste.

Strengths: Advanced catalyst development expertise, cost-effective processing temperatures, strong research foundation with innovative approaches. Weaknesses: Limited to organic waste fractions, technology primarily at research and pilot scale, requires further development for commercial deployment.

Eni SpA

Technical Solution: Eni has developed an integrated waste-to-SAF approach combining advanced waste management with their proprietary Ecofining technology. The process involves converting organic municipal waste through hydrothermal liquefaction to produce bio-crude oil, which is then upgraded using their established refining infrastructure. Eni's technology can process various waste streams including food waste, paper, and organic municipal solid waste, converting them into drop-in sustainable aviation fuel that meets ASTM D7566 specifications. Their approach leverages existing refinery infrastructure and can achieve conversion efficiencies of approximately 60-70% from organic waste to final fuel products. The company has integrated this technology into their traditional refining operations, enabling cost-effective scaling.

Strengths: Utilizes existing refinery infrastructure for cost efficiency, proven Ecofining technology platform, strong integration with traditional energy operations. Weaknesses: Limited to organic waste fractions, requires significant preprocessing, dependent on existing fossil fuel infrastructure.

Core Technologies in High-Quality SAF Production

Conversion of municipal waste to useful oils

A process involving the heating of municipal waste containing polymeric materials in a mixture of hydrogen sulfide and hydrogen at moderate temperatures and pressures in a pressurized reaction vessel, converting the waste into liquid hydrocarbon materials suitable for fractionation into gasoline, diesel fuel, and gas oils, with the ability to handle cellulosic and proteinaceous materials and extraneous organic materials.

Process and system for converting solid municipal waste by depolymerisation and transient multi-step reactions

PatentWO2025215278A1

Innovation

A method and system for treating waste through depolymerization and pyrogasification, involving pretreatment, degassing to remove chlorine, and controlled depolymerization under oxygen-free conditions, followed by gas cleaning and oil distillation, using a series of interrelated devices to produce fuel and by-products without residues.

Environmental Regulations and Policy Framework

The regulatory landscape for converting municipal waste into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) operates within a complex framework of environmental standards, waste management protocols, and aviation fuel specifications. Current regulations primarily focus on waste-to-energy processes under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) in the United States, which establishes guidelines for municipal solid waste handling, treatment, and conversion technologies. The European Union's Waste Framework Directive and Renewable Energy Directive II provide similar regulatory foundations, emphasizing waste hierarchy principles and renewable fuel targets.

Aviation fuel certification represents a critical regulatory component, governed by ASTM International standards and the Federal Aviation Administration's rigorous approval processes. The ASTM D7566 specification defines acceptable synthetic fuel pathways, including waste-derived feedstocks, while maintaining strict quality and performance requirements. International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards further influence global SAF adoption through carbon offsetting mechanisms and sustainability criteria.

Environmental impact assessments constitute mandatory regulatory requirements for waste-to-SAF facilities, addressing air quality standards, greenhouse gas emissions, and potential environmental justice concerns. The Clean Air Act and National Environmental Policy Act establish comprehensive evaluation frameworks for industrial facilities processing municipal waste streams.

Policy incentives significantly shape the regulatory environment through renewable fuel standards, carbon pricing mechanisms, and tax credits. The Renewable Fuel Standard program provides volumetric mandates for advanced biofuels, while state-level low carbon fuel standards create additional market drivers. The Inflation Reduction Act introduced enhanced tax incentives for SAF production, particularly from waste feedstocks.

Emerging regulatory trends indicate increasing focus on lifecycle carbon accounting, circular economy principles, and technology-neutral sustainability criteria. Regulatory harmonization efforts between aviation authorities and environmental agencies aim to streamline approval processes while maintaining environmental protection standards. Future policy developments likely will emphasize performance-based regulations rather than prescriptive technology mandates, enabling innovation in waste-to-SAF conversion pathways.

Economic Feasibility and Cost Analysis

The economic feasibility of converting municipal waste into sustainable aviation fuel hinges on several critical cost components and revenue streams. Capital expenditure represents the most significant initial barrier, with waste-to-SAF facilities requiring investments ranging from $200-500 million depending on processing capacity and technology selection. These facilities typically process 500-2000 tons of municipal solid waste daily, with economies of scale becoming apparent at higher throughput levels.

Operational expenses constitute approximately 60-70% of total production costs, encompassing feedstock procurement, energy consumption, catalyst replacement, and labor. Municipal waste feedstock costs vary significantly by region, ranging from negative costs where tipping fees apply ($20-80 per ton) to positive costs in areas with established waste management systems. Energy requirements for thermochemical conversion processes represent 25-35% of operational costs, though waste heat recovery systems can reduce this burden substantially.

Production costs for waste-derived SAF currently range between $3.50-6.00 per gallon, compared to conventional jet fuel at $2.50-3.50 per gallon. However, government incentives significantly improve economic viability. The U.S. Renewable Fuel Standard provides credits worth $1.50-2.50 per gallon, while the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Grand Challenge offers additional tax incentives. European markets benefit from carbon pricing mechanisms that add $0.80-1.20 per gallon value to SAF.

Revenue optimization depends on multiple product streams beyond SAF production. Integrated facilities can generate electricity from non-convertible waste fractions, produce biochar for carbon sequestration markets, and recover metals for recycling. These co-products can contribute 15-25% of total revenue, improving overall project economics.

Break-even analysis indicates that facilities achieving 70% capacity utilization with feedstock costs below $30 per ton can reach profitability within 8-12 years under current incentive structures. Sensitivity analysis reveals that SAF selling price and feedstock availability represent the most critical variables affecting project viability, while technological improvements reducing conversion costs by 20-30% could achieve grid parity with conventional fuels by 2030.

Speech by Acting CE at Greenway 2026 - Driving Sustainability Through Innovation (English only)

Speech by Acting CE at Greenway 2026 - Driving Sustainability Through Innovation (English only)

******************************************************************************

Following is the speech by the Acting Chief Executive, Mr Paul Lam, SC, at Greenway 2026 - Driving Sustainability Through Innovation today (June 23):

Ambassador Rouse (Ambassador and Head of Office of the European Union to Hong Kong and Macao, Mr Harvey Rouse), Mr Hack (Chair of the European Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, Mr Johannes Hack), Consulate Generals, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen,

Good morning. It is my great pleasure to join you today to open the Greenway 2026. I would like to begin by extending my warmest congratulations to the European Union Office to Hong Kong and Macao and the European Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong on holding the fifth edition of this flagship event.

The growth of this flagship forum into a full-day programme speaks volumes about the importance and imminence of this year's theme, namely, "Driving Sustainability Through Innovation".

On the one hand, environmental challenges, particularly those caused by climate change, have become more acute. Last year, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned that there would be a 70 per cent chance for the five-year average global temperature for 2025 to 2029 to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius - a sharp rise from the 47 per cent forecast just a year earlier. Earlier this month, the WMO reported an 80 per cent likelihood of El Niño developing between June and August, with the probability of it continuing until at least November near or above 90 per cent. As the United Nations Secretary-General warned, El Niño conditions will "pour fuel on the fire of a warming world". In fact, both Europe and Hong Kong as well as other parts of the world are experiencing more extreme weather conditions recently.

To tackle the serious environmental challenges, both the European Union and Hong Kong have set vital goals towards achieving climate neutrality. Insofar as Hong Kong is concerned, we aim at halving our carbon emissions before 2035 from the 2005 level, with a view to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. I am pleased to say that substantial progress has been made: Hong Kong's total greenhouse gas emissions have already fallen by 27 per cent from their 2014 peak.

What is critical is that we shall attempt to achieve these vital goals by taking measures that would be conducive to sustainable economic and social development at the same time. In the Chinese language, crisis is 危機. It consists of two characters: the literal translation of the first one is danger whereas that of the second is opportunity. Ancient wisdom teaches us that danger is always followed by opportunity. The big question is how to seize the opportunity. In the present context, I believe the answer lies in the word "innovation".

This is indeed the overall strategy of Hong Kong as demonstrated by various policy directions and key proposals set out in the public consultation document regarding the First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the HKSAR (Hong Kong Special Administrative Region) (First Five-Year Plan) released last Monday on June 15. Paragraph 6 in Part 6 is titled "New energy, green technology, and innovative applications". It consists of three main directions and related proposals, which are of particular relevance to today's theme:

(a) first, to dovetail with the country's development in new energy technology by supporting and piloting technologies and solutions related to energy management, green buildings, waste treatment, environmental monitoring, and climate risk management;

(b) second, to support the R&D (research and development), production and application of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and hydrogen fuel, promote the low-carbon transition of the aviation industry and the traffic and transport sector, and develop Hong Kong into a demonstration platform for green and low-carbon hydrogen technologies; and

(c) third, to strengthen collaboration across industry, academic and research sectors to promote the local application of technological outcomes achieved by higher education and research institutions, and facilitate the expansion and strengthening of promising green technology enterprises through financial and market-driven mechanisms.

In addition, in Part 2 of the consultation document which sets out directions and proposals on strengthening Hong Kong's development in four major sectors, namely finance, trade, maritime and aviation, apart from referring to green finance, it is stated that Hong Kong needs to promote green transformation to enhance the added value and competitiveness of its maritime and aviation sectors such as the expansion of green fuel bunkering.

I would like to take the opportunity to elaborate on three specific examples to demonstrate Hong Kong's ability and determination in driving sustainability through innovation.

First, green finance. As a leading international financial centre, Hong Kong is Asia's premier sustainable financial hub. The green transformation requires capital inputs on an unprecedented scale, and Hong Kong provides a most reliable and friendly platform for raising the capital needed. For eight consecutive years, Hong Kong has led Asia in arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances, which accounted for about 40 per cent of the regional total. On May 8 this year, the HKSAR Government announced the successful pricing of approximately HK$27.6 billion worth of green bonds and infrastructure bonds denominated under the Government Sustainable Bond Programme and the Infrastructure Bond Programme. They included a EUR750 million 8-year green tranche priced at 3.119 per cent. The HKSAR Government published its Green Bond Framework in March 2019, which was updated in February 2022. It sets out how green bond proceeds will be used to fund projects to improve the environment and facilitate the transition to a low carbon economy. As at August 31, 2025, the Government had successfully issued around HK$240 billion, or US$31 billion, worth of green bonds.

Second, SAF. As an international aviation hub, Hong Kong is committed to supporting the decarbonisation of global flights. SAF can reduce lifecycle emissions by more than 80 per cent as compared with conventional aviation fuel. Recently, in early May, the Government supported a local enterprise, namely EcoCeres, in signing a Memorandum of Understanding with the Dongguan Government to build SAF production plants in Dongguan, a city in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. Incubated and founded in Hong Kong, EcoCeres uses proprietary integrated technology to convert waste cooking oil into internationally certified SAF. The partnership will create an integrated end-to-end model: that is waste-based feedstock collection across the Greater Bay Area, refining and production in Dongguan, and blending, refuelling, and trading operations in Hong Kong - while also helping to drive the development of the regional circular economy.

Third, clean energy and hydrogen. The Government announced the Strategy of Hydrogen Development in Hong Kong in 2024. We are rolling out real-world hydrogen applications, underpinned by robust safety regulations and a certification system designed to recognise green hydrogen. As at the end of May 2026, the Inter-departmental Working Group on Using Hydrogen as Fuel has given agreement-in-principle to 38 hydrogen energy trial projects, covering applications in the areas of transport, infrastructure, and hydrogen gensets at construction sites, etc. The Gas Safety (Amendment) Ordinance 2025 was gazetted on July 25, 2025. The Government is currently drafting the relevant subsidiary legislation. The aim is to provide a clear legal framework and a stable regulatory environment for the hydrogen energy industry, so that local and international investors can develop hydrogen-related businesses in Hong Kong with greater confidence.

There is no doubt that sustainable development by innovation will play a key role in the future development of Hong Kong, and feature prominently in Hong Kong's First Five-Year Plan. This is why I believe that the timing of this forum is perfect. It is most exciting to see so many eminent speakers from different areas who will share their wisdoms with us very soon.

Whether a place can attain sustainable development by innovation would depend very much on its overall competitiveness. In the latest World Competitiveness Yearbook 2026 published by the International Institute for Management Development (IMD), the rule of law was put at the centre of competitiveness. The Director of IMD World Competitiveness Center remarked that economic competitiveness in 2026 is no longer mainly a contest of cost or scale, or even of innovation; it is a contest of institutional credibility. The more fragmented the world becomes, the more valuable predictable rules, and enforceable commitments become. And hence, economies at the top of the table are those that uphold the rule of law most consistently.

This year, Hong Kong's ranking has risen for three consecutive years to the second globally. This is a very strong testament to Hong Kong's institutional credibility under the principle of "one country, two systems" based on the rule of law, and characterised by predictability, reliability, integrity and efficiency.

I would say that another crucial reason for Hong Kong's competitiveness is its openness. Hong Kong is committed to remaining an open and diversified society. For the present purpose, friends from the European Union are most welcome to join hands with us to explore and seize the opportunities offered by using innovation to support a sustainable development whilst overcoming environmental challenges at the same time. Indeed, we have to work together because what is at stake is not merely the interests of the people of the European Union or Hong Kong, but mankind as a whole; and failure is not an option.

May I conclude by wishing you all a productive and inspiring Greenway 2026. Thank you.

The aviation fuel industry operates under a comprehensive framework of regulatory standards that directly impact SAF processing temperature optimization strategies. International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) standards, particularly ICAO Annex 16 Volume IV, establish fundamental requirements for alternative aviation fuels, including specific quality parameters that must be maintained regardless of processing conditions. These standards mandate that SAF must meet identical performance characteristics to conventional Jet A-1 fuel, creating strict boundaries within which temperature optimization must occur.

ASTM D7566 serves as the primary specification governing SAF production and quality control in North America. This standard defines critical fuel properties including density, viscosity, freezing point, and thermal stability limits that are directly influenced by processing temperatures. The specification requires SAF to demonstrate equivalent performance to petroleum-based jet fuel across temperature ranges from -47°C to 300°C, establishing operational constraints for processing temperature selection. Compliance with ASTM D7566 necessitates rigorous testing protocols that validate fuel performance under various thermal conditions.

European regulatory frameworks, primarily governed by EASA certification requirements and EN 15940 standards, impose additional constraints on SAF processing methodologies. These regulations emphasize lifecycle sustainability metrics alongside traditional performance parameters, requiring producers to demonstrate that temperature optimization strategies do not compromise environmental benefits. The European approach integrates carbon intensity calculations with fuel quality assessments, creating a dual optimization challenge for processing temperature selection.

Regulatory compliance monitoring systems require continuous documentation of processing parameters, including temperature profiles throughout production cycles. Quality assurance protocols mandate statistical process control methods that track temperature variations and their correlation with fuel yield and quality metrics. These requirements necessitate sophisticated process monitoring systems capable of real-time temperature adjustment while maintaining regulatory compliance boundaries.

Future regulatory developments indicate increasing emphasis on sustainability metrics and lifecycle assessments in SAF certification processes. Emerging standards are expected to incorporate more stringent requirements for process efficiency and waste minimization, potentially favoring temperature optimization strategies that maximize yield while reducing energy consumption. Regulatory bodies are also developing frameworks for novel feedstock pathways, which may require adaptive temperature optimization approaches to meet evolving compliance requirements.

Environmental Impact of SAF Processing Efficiency

The environmental implications of SAF processing efficiency are fundamentally tied to the optimization of processing temperatures, creating a complex relationship between operational parameters and ecological impact. Temperature optimization directly influences the carbon footprint of SAF production facilities, as higher processing temperatures typically require increased energy consumption, leading to elevated greenhouse gas emissions from utility systems.

Processing efficiency improvements through temperature optimization significantly reduce waste generation across multiple streams. When temperatures are precisely controlled to maximize yield, the volume of unusable byproducts decreases substantially, minimizing disposal requirements and associated environmental burdens. This reduction in waste streams directly correlates with decreased land use for waste management facilities and reduced potential for soil and groundwater contamination.

Energy consumption patterns in SAF processing facilities demonstrate strong sensitivity to temperature control strategies. Optimized temperature profiles can reduce overall energy demand by 15-25% compared to non-optimized operations, translating to proportional reductions in fossil fuel consumption for process heating and cooling systems. This energy efficiency improvement extends beyond direct processing to encompass auxiliary systems including heat exchangers, cooling towers, and waste heat recovery units.

Water resource utilization represents another critical environmental dimension affected by processing efficiency. Temperature optimization reduces the need for excessive cooling water circulation and minimizes thermal pollution discharge to water bodies. Efficient temperature management also decreases the frequency of equipment cleaning cycles, reducing chemical consumption and wastewater generation volumes.

Air quality impacts from SAF processing facilities are substantially influenced by temperature optimization strategies. Lower processing temperatures, when feasible for maintaining yield targets, reduce volatile organic compound emissions and minimize the formation of secondary atmospheric pollutants. Additionally, optimized temperature control reduces the likelihood of thermal decomposition reactions that can generate harmful air emissions.

The lifecycle environmental assessment of temperature-optimized SAF processing reveals cascading benefits throughout the production chain. Improved processing efficiency reduces the feedstock requirements per unit of SAF produced, thereby decreasing the environmental pressure on agricultural systems and reducing land use change impacts. This optimization also enhances the overall sustainability profile of SAF as a renewable fuel alternative, strengthening its position as an environmentally beneficial aviation fuel solution.

text:
In 2017, after a decade of losses and reputation-damaging disasters, Malaysia Airlines was on the verge of bankruptcy.

But almost a decade later, it has delivered its fourth consecutive year of substantial operating profit.

And, while the conflict in the Middle East has heavily impacted the global airline industry, it is benefiting many Asian carriers as they turn to Asian and Australian markets.

Malaysia Airlines is gaining traction in the premium cabin as travellers look for alternatives to Qatar Airways and Emirates.

The ultimate aim of Malaysia Airlines’ Long-Term Business Plan 3.0, which started this year, is for the airline to be in Skytrax’s Top 10 Global Airlines by 2030. It was 27th when the plan was announced.

It aims to achieve this by enhancing customer service experience, operational reliability and upgrading its fleet. The Malaysia Aviation Group has employed an additional 2000 staff over the past four years of profitability, with plans to continue growing its team.

Australia has benefited from a fleet expansion of 22 new-generation aircraft. All cities except Perth have new Airbus A330neo flying to and from Kuala Lumpur from August 2026.

FUELLING SPECULATION

Reliability and fuel security are a big roadblock for expanding airlines as the world continues to face an uncertain future.

But Malaysia Airlines has a secret weapon — Petronas.

Petronas is Malaysia’s state-owned oil and gas company, working in partnership with Malaysia Aviation Group to keep the global fuel crisis from affecting their brand.

Petronas can provide undisturbed fuel supply to Malaysia Aviation Group through their efforts in making Sustainable Aviation Fuel which Malaysia Airlines began using in September 2025.

It is an important step not only towards the country’s goal to be net-zero by 2050, but also in offering reliability to Malaysia Airlines customers.

title: Brazil Could Become Leading SAF Hub: IATA - Mexico Business News
description:
Brazil has one of the largest biomass feedstock potentials globally, estimated at 180 million tonnes by 2050, capable of producing around 60 million tonnes of SAF.
By 2030, sustainably sourced sugar-based ethanol, virgin oils, and waste oils could reach 18 million tonnes of feedstock, translating into roughly 12 million tonnes of SAF production potential.
This is about five times the estimated global SAF output in 2026 of 2.4 million tonnes.
Willie Walsh, Director General, IATA, said Brazil has the conditions to become a global SAF powerhouse, citing its clean electricity mix, feedstock availability, and biofuel expertise.
It argued that reinvestment is necessary to scale SAF production and support emerging technologies that are not yet commercially viable.
text:
The International Air Transport Association (IATA) used its 82nd Annual General Meeting in Rio de Janeiro to highlight Brazil’s potential to become a global sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production hub, citing its biomass resources, ethanol industry, and refining base as key drivers of aviation decarbonization. IATA said airlines will require around 500 million tonnes of SAF to achieve net-zero CO₂ emissions by 2050, placing significant pressure on global supply expansion. Brazil has one of the largest biomass feedstock potentials globally, estimated at 180 million tonnes by 2050, capable of producing around 60 million tonnes of SAF.

By 2030, sustainably sourced sugar-based ethanol, virgin oils, and waste oils could reach 18 million tonnes of feedstock, translating into roughly 12 million tonnes of SAF production potential. This is about five times the estimated global SAF output in 2026 of 2.4 million tonnes. The country has around 15 SAF projects under development, which could deliver about 2 million tonnes of capacity if completed.

Willie Walsh, Director General, IATA, said Brazil has the conditions to become a global SAF powerhouse, citing its clean electricity mix, feedstock availability, and biofuel expertise.

“Brazil has all the ingredients to be a global SAF powerhouse. It has one of the cleanest electricity mixes and abundant feedstock. As a major biofuel producer, it has infrastructure and experience. Brazil can lead aviation decarbonization, create jobs, reduce fossil fuel dependence, and grow the economy. With the right policy sequencing, Brazil can start this market,” he said.

IATA said Brazil’s ethanol production experience and refining base provide competitive advantages that could support scaling of HEFA and ethanol-to-jet pathways, as well as enable potential SAF exports. The association added that this industrial base could expand across agriculture, logistics, refining, and fuel production, supporting jobs and energy security.

The organization also said scaling SAF production in Brazil will require investment in infrastructure, conversion technologies, and logistics systems linking feedstock supply to production facilities. It stressed that policy incentives, financing mechanisms, and alignment with global sustainability standards will be necessary to unlock scale. IATA added that a book-and-claim system and SAF certificates under Brazil’s “Fuel of the Future” framework could support market development and align with CORSIA.

Marie Owens Thomsen, Senior Vice President for Sustainability and Chief Economist, IATA, said policy sequencing and alignment with global frameworks are essential for Brazil to achieve scale.

“Brazil has strong advantages in resources and experience that could place it at the center of SAF markets. The economic gains could be significant. Policies must follow the correct sequence to reach scale and reduce costs. Skipping supply chain development and moving directly to mandates will not work. Alignment with global standards such as CORSIA is necessary,” she said.

According to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), SAF, hydrogen, and electrification currently account for less than 1% of global aviation fuel use. The OECD International Transport Forum estimates that air freight represents less than 1% of global freight but generates emissions around 20 times higher per ton-kilometer than other transport modes.

IATA said these findings underscore the need for coordinated global policy to avoid overlapping measures that increase costs without delivering additional environmental benefits. It added that Brazil’s opportunity depends on timely investment, policy alignment, and the development of scalable production systems. Industry participants said Brazil could become a net SAF exporter if current projects are completed and policy support is sustained.

IATA also said European policy frameworks should ensure revenues from emissions trading systems are reinvested into aviation decarbonization rather than absorbed into general budgets. It argued that reinvestment is necessary to scale SAF production and support emerging technologies that are not yet commercially viable. The association added that overlapping regulatory measures can increase costs and reduce investment certainty for airlines operating international networks, stressing the need for alignment with global mechanisms such as CORSIA to ensure consistent emissions accounting.

Industry data shows SAF production reached 1.9 million tonnes in 2025, equal to about 0.6% of global jet fuel demand. It is projected to rise to 2.4 million tonnes in 2026, or 0.8% of demand. SAF costs remain two to five times higher than conventional jet fuel depending on region and incentives, while limited feedstock availability and technology maturity continue to constrain supply expansion.

Analysts said regions with lower-cost renewable electricity such as Brazil, India, the Middle East, and North Africa hold structural advantages for e-SAF production. However, investment has remained concentrated in higher-cost jurisdictions due to policy incentives. Industry participants said this mismatch between economics and policy signals has slowed final investment decisions in Europe and other advanced markets.
